articles.title: ‘They’re selling the safety of the traveling public’: TSA workers decry Trump privatization push
articles.text:
The labor union representing workers at the Transportation Security Administration (TSA) is raising alarms over a new program that will expand privatizing security checkpoints at three airports.

The agency informed the union last month of plans to enact the TSA Gold+ program, which would shift security and control of the screening technology into the hands of private contractors at airports in Tampa, Charleston and Des Moines. Union workers are expected to lose their union contract and benefits once a contractor takes over.

“This is a major departure and step backwards from the aviation screening security system that Congress created in the wake of the September 11 terrorist attacks in 2001 and the deadly bombing of Pan Am flight 103 over Scotland in 1988,” Everett Kelley, national president of the American Federation of Government Employees (AFGE) said in statement.

“Changes of this magnitude should not be made behind closed doors without the input of Congress, the flying public, the local airport authorities and TSA employees themselves.”

The AFGE is currently reviewing legal options to fight back against the privatization push from the Trump administration.

Before the TSA was created in November 2001 by the Bush administration after the 9/11 attacks, airport security was operated by private contractors with less stringent standards.

Chris Finlay, a TSA worker in Tampa and president of AFGE local 556, recounted his experience working at another Florida airport where, 12 years ago, a private contractor took over screening. At the time, TSA agents were told their salary would remain the same – only for the contractor to cut pay a few weeks into employment.

“For a private contract company, they’re not doing it out of duty for the traveling public or the constitution or anything. They’re doing it because it’s a business decision,” Finlay said.

“As a business, their primary goal is to be profitable, and staffing is the most expensive part of that contract, so if they can reduce how much they have to pay staff, they’re going to.”

He also noted concerns over security quality. In 2015, an employee working for the private contractor at the Florida airport outside Orlando was fired after they reported a steak knife made it through security to the contractor.

“A private company is going to be concerned with being profitable,” Finlay said. “They’re selling the safety of the traveling public for corporate greed. That’s what is happening.”

Gold+ is the latest TSA privatization effort, adding on to other initiatives, including an expansion of the screening partnership program that uses private contractors, overseen by the TSA, to handle security screenings at small and non-hub airports. The TSA plans to eliminate roughly 4,500 positions as the program expands to 220 US airports.

While the program has private contractors managing screening, unlike Gold+, it does not allow the contractors to own and operate security equipment.

In May, the TSA deputy administrator, Adam Stahl, said that the Gold+ privatization push could eventually include artificial intelligence replacing some security officers.

The changes come in the wake of the Trump administration’s proposed TSA budget cuts for fiscal year 2027, which would entail eliminating 8,400 transportation security officer positions, about 14% of the TSA screening workforce.

Last year, the Trump administration tried to eliminate collective bargaining agreements for 47,000 TSA employees – first in March and again in December, though the efforts were blocked by federal judges.

“The Trump administration’s clear objective is to ultimately privatize all aviation security screening functions, and we don’t have to theorize about what that may look like because we have been through this before and witnessed the devastating and deadly consequences,” Kelley said.

TSA officers will have first right of refusal to move their employment, and affected employees will either receive severance or retirement based on their years of service with agency.

“TSA Gold+ presents a new way for TPA [Tampa international airport] to deliver exceptional service to every traveler, while advancing security, efficiency, and the overall airport experience. Throughout this transition, we remain committed to operational stability and supporting our employees,” said a TSA spokesperson in an email.

“We look forward to working closely with TPA to implement enhancements that will benefit everyone who travels through this airport.”

articles.title: Joe Marler: Traitors star to become BBC's first celebrity Gladiator
articles.text:
Former rugby star Joe Marler is to become the first ever celebrity Gladiator on the BBC's popular entertainment series.

The 36-year-old, who also took part in the first series of Celebrity Traitors, will be known as Mauler and face contenders when the fourth series of Gladiators begins in 2027.

"Mauler will see you now," Marler said in a video posted on Instagram, external announcing the news, recorded in the Gladiators dressing room.

The BBC said Marler will make his debut with a series of "special appearances packed with power, personality and plenty of surprises".

Filming for the fourth series is currently under way in Sheffield, the BBC confirmed in a statement.

"Known for his uncompromising style of play and larger-than-life sense of humour, Joe has built a reputation as one of the UK's most entertaining sporting personalities," the corporation said.

"Now, he's taking on an entirely new challenge as he joins the ranks of the Gladiators, bringing his trademark physicality and competitive spirit to one of television's toughest arenas."

The former England rugby international star, who is from Heathfield, Sussex, will join fellow Gladiators such as Nitro, Viper, Diamond and Sabre in batle when the show returns next year.

Gladiators was a hugely successful show on ITV in the 1990s, and saw members of the public take on a group of elite athletes who each had their own on-screen persona.

Olympic swimmer Sharron Davies, who like Marler was already known as a famous sports personality, joined that iteration of the show in 1995 as the character Amazon.

The format was revived by Sky for two series in 2008, before the current iteration launched in 2024, quickly becoming a hit for BBC One.

A celebrity spin-off is separately in the works, featuring contestants including presenter AJ Odudu, comedian Sara Pascoe, podcaster Chris Ramsey and social media star George Clarke.

articles.title: David Ellison breaks silence on Paramount-Warner Bros mega merger
articles.text:
Paramount Skydance chief executive David Ellison has broken his silence, defending his company's $110bn (£86bn) takeover of Warner Bros. Discovery.

Opposition to the mega-merger relies on a vision of Hollywood that "no longer exists," he wrote in an op-ed published by The New York Times.

In his first public comments on the transaction, Ellison rejected claims that a combined media giant would exert excessive control over the market or erode newsroom independence.

The public intervention comes as Paramount and Warner Bros. continue an intense legal battle to close their massive deal, which was recently put on hold.

Addressing concerns over the future of Paramount's CBS and Warner's CNN, Ellison insisted the news outlets would remain non-partisan and stay positioned to "tell it straight down the middle."

To counter antitrust concerns, Ellison pointed out that a merged Paramount-Warner would account for less than 20% of US television watch time – dropping to around 13% when accounting for YouTube – as it competes against tech giants like Netflix, Amazon, and Apple whose resources "dwarf ours."

He also highlighted commitments to expand traditional production, promising 30 theatrical films and 170 television series annually backed by more than $30bn in annual content investment.

Scaling up content investment is vital to sustain creative workers against technology platforms driven by engagement algorithms, he argued.

Even so, Ellison acknowledged that "nobody can dictate what audiences will love."

The legal battle escalated in July when 12 state attorneys generals, led by California's Rob Bonta, alongside the Writers Guild of America, filed antitrust lawsuits to halt the merger. They argued that the merger would violate the Clayton Act by reducing competition and harming opportunities for writers.

articles.title: Disney agrees deal to let TikTokers use its characters in videos
articles.text:
Disney and TikTok have agreed a deal which will allow creators to use clips from Disney films, including its subsidiaries, in their videos.

It means clips from hit franchises like Star Wars, Toy Story and the Marvel Cinematic Universe will soon start popping up in videos - which will also be shared on Disney's short-form video platform, Verts.

The scheme will be launched in the US before being rolled out to other countries.

Neither company shared financial details of the agreement, although it follows the collapse of a $1bn (£745m) deal between Disney and OpenAI which would have let people use its characters in AI-generated videos.

That agreement was cancelled in March when OpenAI shut down its AI video generation tool Sora, citing a decision to focus on other parts of its business.

"Today, fans are celebrating our stories in entirely new ways," said Disney's chief marketing and brand officer Asad Ayaz, following the TikTok deal being announced.

In a joint statement, Disney and TikTok said audience engagement on social media, including videos created by fans, was playing an "increasingly important role" in the entertainment world.

TikTok said its platform saw an average of 6.5 million posts relating to film and TV per day last year.

Fans like to use clips from films and TV shows in their videos, but without express permission, they would often be taken down due to copyright claims.

This makes it harder for a wide audience to engage with fan-created content around a big release.

Disney and TikTok said a jointly-run programme would boost some creators' videos and give them access to exclusive events.

Online creators and influencers are becoming more important to brands' marketing strategies.

Last year, a report from Oxford Economics said YouTube content creators contributed £2.2bn to the UK economy in 2024 and supported 45,000 jobs.

There is also a recognition that even very small influencers, who focus on niche topics, might have lower follower counts but come with a hyper-engaged audience.

Disney launched its short form video platform Verts in the US in March, with plans to expand that further around the world.

articles.title: Perez Hilton recovering in hospital after self-harming during TikTok livestream
articles.text:
US blogger Perez Hilton is recovering in hospital after members of the public reported that he had appeared to self-harm during a TikTok livestream.

Emergency services were called to his home in Miami on Tuesday after concerned viewers reported a man "livestreaming acts of self-harm on social media".

The Miami-Dade Sheriff's Office told US media that an individual had been "safely recovered" and taken to "a local hospital, where he is receiving medical attention".

Police added that their crisis response unit and licensed mental health professionals were also "on scene providing support and resources to the individual's family".

Hilton, whose real name is Mario Lavandeira, was home alone during the time of the live stream, police confirmed, and had his TikTok account suspended soon after.

In a statement issued to BBC News the Miami sheriff's office did not name Hilton but confirmed they had attended to reports of a man harming himself.

"Deputies quickly located the individual's residence, where they spoke with family members on scene, and confirmed he was alone inside," police said.

After assessing the situation, officers decided to "tactically disengage while continuing to monitor the situation and providing the needed support to his family", police said.

"In many incidents involving a person experiencing a mental health crisis or actively harming themselves, deputies prioritise de-escalation by creating time, distance and opportunities for communication," their statement said.

"Unless there is an immediate threat to others, slowing the situation and utilizing crisis intervention techniques can reduce the likelihood of a suicide-by-cop encounter and minimise the risk of injury to the individual, deputies and the public."

Suicide by cop is a US term for when individuals try to end their lives by behaving in a way that will provoke police into killing them.

In a later update, the Sheriff's Office said the man had been "safely recovered and transported by Miami-Dade Fire Rescue to a local hospital, where he is receiving medical attention"

They added: "The Miami-Dade Sheriff's Office Crisis Response Unit and Licensed Mental Health Professionals are also on scene providing support and resources to the individual's family."

BBC News has asked representatives for Hilton for comment, and also contacted TikTok and Miami police.

articles.title: Graeme Hall: Presenter and dog trainer joins Strictly Come Dancing line-up
articles.text:
Presenter and dog trainer Graeme Hall is the latest star to join the line-up for this year's Strictly Come Dancing.

Known as the Dogfather, Hall has appeared on Channel 5's Dog's Behaving (Very) Badly since the show's launch in 2017.

He also fronted The Dog Hospital and contributed to BBC radio programmes, ITV's This Morning, and wrote a regular column for the Times.

In a statement, Hall said: "I can't believe I am joining the cast of Strictly for 2026. I have always loved dancing, so to have the opportunity to learn from the best in the business is a dream come true."

He added: "I have watched the show for years, so to be a part of it feels like a very exciting challenge, albeit more than a bit nerve-wracking! I can't wait to get started. Bring it on!"

Hall has also written books including The Ultimate Kid's Guide to Dogs and previously made a cameo appearance in the hit drama All Creatures Great and Small.

Dogs Behaving Badly launched on Channel 4 in 2017, before moving to Channel 5 two years later with a slight change of title.

Hall is the 11th celebrity to be confirmed for this year's series, joining stars including Delta Goodrem, Lacey Turner, Dani Dyer, Will Best, Jaime Winstone and Dame Sarah Storey.

More contestants are set to be announced in the coming weeks, with 15 expected in the final line-up. Scroll down to see the rest of this year's line-up so far:

Other celebrities to be confirmed for Strictly this year include former England and Manchester City winger Shaun Wright-Phillips.

The football pundit, who is the son of Arsenal legend Ian Wright, had 36 caps for England and also played for clubs including Chelsea and Queens Park Rangers.

His fancy footwork may have dazzled on the pitch but Wright-Phillips said this latest challenge "is definitely outside my comfort zone".

"Dancing is in my blood - but mainly at family events!" he said. "I'm super excited to get started and really looking forward to the challenge!"

While ex-footballers have had mixed fortunes on previous Strictly series, former soccer star Karen Carney flipped the script last year by winning the coveted glitterball.

Antonia has portrayed dragon-rider Lady Baela Targaryen in HBO's Game of Thrones prequel since 2022. She is currently starring as Eurydice in the Tony Award-winning musical Hadestown in London's West End.

Her acting career began when she was 14 when she appeared in a short film adaptation of The Tempest, before being cast as a guest role in the BBC's Doctors.

The singer and actress has also appeared in series including Nolly, Stay Close, Stath Lets Flats, and Doctor Who.

Antonia said: "I can't quite believe that I will be heading to the Strictly ballroom this September! I have grown up watching Strictly, and I am so excited to take the challenge on and (hopefully!) learn a new skill. See you on the dancefloor!"

Jaime Winstone launched her acting career in 2004 and her film credits include Bullet Boy, Tomb Raider and Wild Bill, as well stage productions such as 2:22 A Ghost Story.

The actress, who also won acclaim for her portrayal of Barbara Windsor in the BBC biopic Babs, said she was "so excited" to be joining the dance competition.

The actress said in a statement she was "no stranger to a dance floor", but added that ballroom is "a whole new world for me".

"I love a challenge though," she continued, "so can't wait to enter my showgirl era and get super sparkly!"

Winstone has also appeared in TV series such as Poirot, Dead Set, Torvill & Dean, Mad Dogs, Count Abdulla and Four Lives.

After playing Windsor in Babs, Winstone stepped into the late actress's famous role of Peggy Mitchell in EastEnders, appearing in flashback specials, most recently in the soap's 40th anniversary last year.

Known as Great Britain's most successful Paralympian of all time, Dame Sarah Storey has secured 19 gold medals across the nine Paralympic Games she competed in.

The swimmer and cyclist said embarking on the challenge is "hugely exciting" and she "can't wait to get started".

"I have always loved watching Strictly and my daughter Louisa is a very talented dancer, so to be able to learn from the best and hopefully understand even more about her world, is incredibly motivating!" she said.

The former athlete won four golds at London 2012. She started her career as a swimmer and later switched to cycling, winning 30 Paralympic medals in total.

Best is known for hosting Big Brother with AJ Odudu on ITV since 2023, and as host of the Hits Radio Breakfast Show alongside Fleur East and James Barr.

He said it was "an absolute dream" to be taking to the BBC One contest's dance floor in September, "albeit a pretty terrifying one".

Best added: "I've been lucky to do lots of live telly before, but absolutely nothing like this. And I cannot wait!

"I have no idea if I can actually dance, but bring on the sequins, bring on the quicksteps, bring on the dance floor! I'm going to try to enjoy every minute of it."

Celebrity hair stylist Chris Appleton is also part of this year's line-up.

Appleton, best known for his work with Kim Kardashian, joins singer-songwriter Delta Goodrem, EastEnders actress Lacey Turner and reality star Dani Dyer in the battle for the Glitterball trophy.

The Leicester-born Color Wow creative director said: "I'm thrilled to be joining Strictly Come Dancing and coming home to the UK for this incredible experience."

He has also created red carpet looks for the likes of Jennifer Lopez, Katy Perry and Ariana Grande, while having his work showcased on the covers of publications including Vogue, Harper's Bazaar and Vanity Fair.

"I've always believed that the best things happen when you take a chance and try something new," added the 43-year-old, who this year released a memoir entitled Your Roots Don't Define You.

"I may know my way around a salon floor, but the dance floor is a whole different story - and I can't wait to get started."

Dani Dyer, the media personality and daughter of actor Danny Dyer appeared in the launch episode last year, but was then injured in training and pulled out before the competition began.

That incident has not put her off trying again. "I am so excited to be back in the ballroom this September," she said.

"I just cannot wait to get my dancing shoes back on and hopefully this time around I can actually make it to week one! I'm just over the moon and cannot wait to find out who else is doing it."

The 29-year-old, who first found fame on Love Island in 2018, fractured her ankle when she "landed funny" in rehearsals with dance partner Nikita Kuzmin before the competitive episodes began last September.

She was replaced by actress Amber Davies, another former Love Island winner, who went on to reach the Strictly final.

Earlier this year, Dyer was joint winner of Channel 4's Celebrity SAS: Who Dares Wins, and appeared with her dad in TV show The Dyers' Caravan Park.

Josh Widdicombe, Emma Willis and Johannes Radebe will take over as Strictly presenters this year, following the departures of Tess Daly and Claudia Winkleman.

The first line-up announcements were made significantly earlier than usual - the BBC usually confirms the line-up in August.

Speaking to ITV's Good Morning Britain in June, Ballas said: "There are going to be some people on there that will make you go 'wow'."

Asked about the new presenting trio, Ballas said she was "very excited to see what they bring" to the show.

"I know they took lots of chemistry tests, as did everybody, and those chemistry tests have brought those three people together, and I believe it's absolutely unbelievable," she said.

Ballas described the number of new elements on this year's show as "quite extraordinary", but added that it will still feel familiar to viewers.

"I don't think they'll change the show too much, maybe tweaks here and there, but no major changes."

Ballas, Craig Revel Horwood, Motsi Mabuse and Anton Du Beke will all return as judges.

Regular pro dancers including Amy Dowden, Dianne Buswell, Katya Jones, Vito Coppola and Aljaz Skorjanec will all be back on the dance floor.

However, professional dancers Gorka Marquez, Nadiya Bychkova, Luba Mushtuk, Karen Hauer and Michelle Tsiakkas will not be returning this year.

articles.title: Belfast Fleadh: Kate Nash on Irish history, heritage and covering Sinéad O'Connor
articles.text:
Singer-songwriter Kate Nash believes many English people are disconnected from parts of their own history, and her latest single is an attempt to start a conversation about why.

She has recorded a cover of Famine, Sinéad O'Connor's 1994 song about one of Ireland's darkest periods, using it to explore wider questions about how Britain's role in the famine is remembered.

For Nash, the project was also deeply personal.

Born in London to an Irish mother, she attended a Catholic school, spent childhood holidays in the Republic of Ireland and the first instrument she learned was the tin whistle, despite long claiming it was the piano.

Revisiting the song more than three decades later, Nash said she was struck not only by its message, but by her little knowledge of the subject matter.

"Sinéad gave me the whole history lesson that school never gave me, that I didn't really get at home either," Nash told BBC News NI ahead of a performance in Belfast as part of this year's Fleadh Cheoil na hÉireann fringe programme.

She is quick to clarify what she means when she says English people do not know their own history.

"When I'm saying the English don't know their history, I'm also English.

"So I'm saying, I don't know my history… and I want to learn."

Nash's debut album Made of Bricks came out in 2007 and spawned her biggest hit, Foundations.

She's since released four more studio albums, including 9 Sad Symphonies in 2024.

While working in the United States more than a decade ago, Kate met music producer Kool Kojak and was encouraged to explore her Irish heritage through music.

After O'Connor's death in 2023, he suggested recording Famine.

"I was like, 'oh my God, that's so audacious, only an American could suggest that'," Nash said.

"But then I thought, why not?

"The tradition of covering old folk songs, passing music through is really important. And the more people that cover that song really the better, because you can bring that message, the education, to a new audience."

Enda Delaney, professor of modern history and director of research at the Edinburgh Futures Institute, believes Nash's point of view is "fair comment".

Unlike in the Republic of Ireland, he said, Anglo-Irish history is not routinely taught to English students, creating a gap in public understanding.

"The fact that one million people died in a part of the United Kingdom, which of course Ireland was in the 1840s... there isn't a really good knowledge of the context in which those terrible events occurred."

He said there should be greater emphasis on Irish history in schools and pointed to growing interest in the subject at university level.

"When you've got two societies which are so closely located to each other and so deeply intertwined, it's really important that both Irish people and British people understand those shared points of history."

Nash said she had discussed the issue with educators and believes they need more support.

"There's a lot of pressure on teachers… they need to be empowered to teach difficult topics," she said.

"Sometimes they rely on lessons they've already developed because they don't have time or resources to introduce new material."

The Department for Education, which oversees the curriculum in English maintained schools, said Ireland and the UK "have a uniquely shared history, relevant not just to the millions of British citizens of Irish descent but the country as a whole".

"The national curriculum provides a core frame within which teachers can take the opportunity to teach about Britain and Ireland in the 19th Century, including the Great Famine," a spokesperson told BBC News NI.

A revitalised curriculum "will go further to strengthen pupils' understanding", they added.

"This will give teachers a clear framework to bring in a wide range of topics, including those that are challenging or uncomfortable."

More than one million people died during the Irish famine between 1845 and 1852, when Ireland was part of the United Kingdom, and about two million emigrated over the following decade.

It was triggered by potato blight which spread across Europe.

In 1997, Tony Blair issued a landmark statement, acknowledging that the British government failed the Irish people during this time.

However it later emerged it was neither written, nor approved by him.

That debate sits at the centre of both O'Connor's and Nash's interpretation of Famine.

Robert Tombs, professor emeritus at the University of Cambridge and founding editor of History Reclaimed, argued the British government relief efforts should be judged against the economic realities of the 1840s.

"If the Irish famine were to be taught, it should counter the myth that it was caused or aggravated by Britain," he said.

While Irish farmers did export some food to Britain, "it was dwarfed by the amount being brought in for distribution by the UK government", he added.

As ministers grappled with high food prices and moved to repeal the Corn Laws, (tariffs on grain that kept the price of bread artificially high), the government, led by Sir Robert Peel, imported large quantities of maize and expanded relief schemes that at one stage fed about three million people a day.

However, the maize proved difficult to mill and distribute.

Campbell explained that second-generation Irish identity is often misunderstood, with artistic expressions of that heritage frequently provoking mixed reactions.

Artists he said, did not simply "decide to become Irish".

"They grew up feeling Irish. It was just an organic sense of identity."

But of the many second-generation, political pop efforts, he said Nash's recent recording stands out for being so "overt".

"She's tackling one of the really big issues in Anglo-Irish politics and history," he said.

"It's quite a brave thing to do."

Nash believes that while many people in England engage with Irish culture, they are avoiding harder conversations about history.

"For English people, it's really important to appreciate more than just the food and the culture and the Guinness," she said.

"We need history, we need context, we need to understand things."

Kate Nash performs at The Mac in Belfast on 6 August as part of the fringe programme for the Fleadh Cheoil na hÉireann.

articles.title: The Mummy film ad banned from London Underground
articles.text:
Posters for the new The Mummy film have been banned from the London Underground and other billboards after regulators said they included realistic depictions of a dead child.

The Advertising Standards Authority (ASA) received 30 complaints regarding the promotional campaign for the Lee Cronin film and said the posters must not be displayed in areas where children could see them.

Many complainants argued the imagery was distressing for both children and adults.

Warner Bros defended the campaign, stating it had been prepared with "due responsibility to consumers and society" and was not designed to create fear or offence.

The poster shows a close-up image of a female figure with a mummified appearance, sunken features and one eye swollen shut, alongside the tagline: "Some things are meant to stay buried."

The distributor explained that the character depicted was a "living mummy" who was returned to her parents as a young adult, many years after having been kidnapped as a child.

It argued that the poster used a neutral facial expression while avoiding elements of violence or intimidation to reduce any risk of distress.

Warner Bros added that the design had been cleared by Transport for London's advertising partner, Global, for display across the London Underground network.

However, the ASA upheld the complaints regarding the outdoor and Underground posters.

The watchdog noted that the figure's grey, ashen skin, cracked lips and fixed, vacant expression combined to give a "realistic impression of a dead child".

The ASA stated: "Because the figure had recognisable human features, we considered that viewers were likely to understand it as a realistic depiction of a dead child."

articles.title: One Show's Alex Jones ‘too scared’ to admit she wanted to be on TV
articles.text:
One Show presenter Alex Jones says she was "too scared" as a young girl to admit she wanted to work in television.

The broadcaster, 49, said growing up in Ammanford, Carmarthenshire, she had never believed such a career would be possible.

"When I was a little girl growing up in south Wales, I thought I'd like to be a presenter, but I was too scared to say anything because nobody in south Wales became broadcasters, especially not on national television," she said.

Jones, who has been hosting the BBC's flagship magazine show since 2010, was fired from two jobs in TV before getting her first break at 21.

Recalling a day when she presented from Windsor Castle, she said: "I really thought about that little girl that day and thought, 'I can't believe that this is what I do for a job'."

She graduated from TV researcher to presenter for BBC's first digital channel, BBC Choice, and then went on to present for the Welsh language channel S4C.

articles.title: Glen Hansard funeral: Bono, Eddie Vedder and Hozier among mourners
articles.text:
Stars from the world of music including U2's Bono, Pearl Jam's lead singer Eddie Vedder, and Hozier, attended the funeral of Glen Hansard on Tuesday.

The 56-year-old Oscar-winning Irish singer and songwriter died in a motorcycle crash in Dublin last week.

Hansard, who shot to prominence in 1991 musical comedy film The Commitments, was long-time frontman of acclaimed rock band The Frames.

News of his sudden death shocked the music world and fans alike, with tributes being paid from the likes of Ed Sheeran and Bruce Springsteen, who said he was "heartbroken".

Many people also paid their respects at a public wake in the city on Monday.

The funeral was held in St Patrick's Cathedral in Dublin on Tuesday and featured musical performances by friends and family.

Mourners included Bono, Eddie Vedder, Hozier, The Edge, Steve Coogan, Imelda May, Paddy Casey, Declan O'Rourke, and Angeline Ball, who starred alongside Hansard in the BAFTA-winning comedy-drama The Commitments.

Representatives of the President of Ireland Catherine Connolly and the Taoiseach (Irish PM) Micheál Martin were also among the mourners.

At the start of the service, a guitar was brought up to the altar by Colm Mac Con Iomaire, a former Frames band member.

Mac Con Iomaire went on to perform a song for those gathered alongside Liam Ó Maonlaí.

Irish traditional musician Breandáin Ó Beaglaoich said Hansard "was so well known on the big stages of Ireland and all over the world".

He described him as an "ordinary kind-hearted Ballymun man.. a true Dub." Ó Beaglaoich also performed a song.

Glen Hansard's widow, the Finnish poet Maire Saaritsa, thanked her late husband "for the life we shared, searching for truth and beauty side by side".

Fighting back tears, she said they found that truth and beauty in their three-year-old son, Christy.

"He cannot be here today, he is too young to witness or understand an event of such scale," she says.

But she added: "The bright spirit he inherited from his father is with us."

Irish superstar Bono recited U2's song A Beautiful Day. As the recital ended he began to sing the song, urging the congregation to join in.

U2's lead guitarist The Edge also attended the service and approached the microphone to join in the version of Beautiful Day as his band-mate Bono finished his recital.

At the end of the service, the coffin left the church to a musical send-off, with mourners inside the building continuing to sing along to a rendition of Bob Dylan's Forever Young.

Hansard's life was steeped in music, from first picking up a guitar as a teenager right until the final hours of his life, when he was performing in a traditional music session.

His career spanned more than three decades, including winning the Academy Award for Best Original Song in 2008 with Marketa Irglova, which featured in the low-budget musical romance film Once.

Following Hansard's death, many people travelled to sign a book of condolence in Temple Bar in Dublin.

And thousands of fans queued to pay tribute to the musician, during his public wake on Monday.

Fans spoke about going to his concerts and seeing him busking on the street.

Danni Rohde, a fan of Hansard's band, The Frames, said it "doesn't feel real".

Another fan, Chris James, said he saw Hansard busking for the first time 25 years ago on Dublin's Grafton Street.

"I thought it one of the coolest things I'd ever seen and one of the reasons I picked up and started playing guitar," he said.

One fan described his death as a loss to Ireland.

articles.title: Ed Sheeran convicted for failing to insure Aston Martin
articles.text:
Ed Sheeran has been convicted and fined for failing to insure his classic Aston Martin while it was being restored and converted to an electric car.

The singer-songwriter sent the the silver 1966 model for an overhaul in 2021, but in December 2025 the DVLA spotted Sheeran had not paid for insurance while restoration work was under way.

Sheeran, 35, told Bradford Magistrates' Court on Friday by letter that he believed the workshop's insurance covered his car and the Aston Martin had not been on the road for the past five years.

But he pleaded guilty to keeping a motor vehicle which does not meet insurance requirements and was ordered to pay a £666 fine, £100 costs and a £266 victim surcharge.

Sheeran was prosecuted by the DVLA in a behind closed doors hearing and submitted a letter of explanation to accompany his guilty plea.

He explained the car "remained within the control of the workshop", based in Durham, since he handed it over in 2021 and had been kept off public roads "at all times".

He also wrote: "There has accordingly been no risk to third party members of the public arising from uninsured driving of the vehicle.

"I have at no point had physical possession or practical control of the vehicle.

"In fact, the vehicle has been inoperable since 2021, through the relevant date and to the present day.

"It is still in the process of being restored and converted into an electric vehicle at the workshop," Sheeran added.

He later apologised for taking up court resources but also insisted he never received the DVLA's initial offer of an out-of-court fine, which he said he would have paid immediately.

Sheeran called it a "genuine administrative misunderstanding" and said the car was declared off-road with a SORN notice on 1 February this year.

As Sheeran's case was dealt with under the Single Justice Procedure system, it could be sent to any magistrates' court regardless of the location of the offence, based on a national database.

He was among 1,451 people across England and Wales to be convicted last week of failing to insure their vehicles.

articles.title: Leicester Comedy Festival under threat as operator ceases trading
articles.text:
The company that ran one of the UK's biggest comedy festivals has ceased trading.

The directors of Big Difference Company - which ran Leicester Comedy Festival - announced "with great sadness" it had become insolvent and ceased trading. It comes weeks after it submitted a serious incident report to the Charity Commission over ongoing financial issues.

The directors of the festival, which started in 1994, cited "increasing costs, a difficult funding environment, and significant pressures within the live comedy sector" as factors in its decision.

Leicester City Council said it would work with promoters and venues "to ensure that an interim comedy festival programme can take place in 2027".

Harry Hill, Matt Lucas, Graham Norton and Sarah Millican are among the well-known names who have performed at the event over the past three decades.

Set up by students from De Montfort University in 1994, Leicester Comedy Festival became a registered company the following year before the firm changed its name to Big Difference in 2009.

"For 32 years, [the festival] has been an important part of the cultural and economic life of our region, showcasing comedy talent, attracting visitors, and supporting local businesses and venues," the directors said.

"We acknowledge that this news will be deeply disappointing to staff, performers, venues, promoters and supporters."

In May it emerged that hundreds of comedians had been unpaid following this year's festival, and in July an arts venue managed by the charity was repossessed due to the "non-payment of rent and insurance".

The directors said they "worked tirelessly to avoid this outcome", including looking at reducing costs and seeking new funding, but said it was "not possible to secure a sustainable future".

"We recognise the significant impact this will have on our employees, performers, venues, suppliers and other creditors, and we are sincerely sorry to all those affected," they said.

"Our immediate focus is to meet our legal obligations and engage constructively with stakeholders throughout the insolvency process.

"Looking ahead, we remain committed to working with stakeholders, including Leicester City Council, funders, venues and the wider community, to explore how a sustainable long-term future can be secured for this much-loved festival."

Geoff Rowe, who helped establish the festival but left in 2023, said he was "sad and angry" for performers, staff and the community.

"I know [Big Difference] has faced challenges, as everyone has in terms of business rates, national insurance and cost of living. But was it inevitable? I'd like to think it wasn't.

"Because there are loads of festivals that are weathering the storm and there are loads of comedy promoters and clubs that have got through it," he said.

"I see Big Difference as being - or were - the guardians of Leicester Comedy Festival but I think there is the potential for someone else to take on that guardianship.

"So maybe there is a bit of optimism there.

"But then I think about the hundreds of people who are owed a significant amount of money from the festival in 2026 and I feel sad and angry all over again."

A statement issued on behalf of former Leicester Comedy Festival staff said they were "stunned and heartbroken" by the development.

"We are so sad. For working comedians, for venues, for audiences, but mostly for Leicester," they said.

"It is our hope of all hopes that Leicester Comedy Festival and The UK Kids' Comedy Festival can live on, with a model that works for all.

"We don't know what that looks like and we know that the future is as uncertain as it could be right now.

"But, we know that there is far too much appetite and history for comedy in Leicester for this to be it."

Leicester city mayor Sir Peter Soulsby said the council would ensure a comedy festival continued to take place.

"We're very sorry that the Big Difference Company has gone into liquidation, and we understand that this is a difficult time for its staff and all of those affected," he said.

"The Leicester Comedy Festival has been a hugely important part of Leicester's cultural calendar, bringing thousands of visitors to the city every year, and with them a big boost to our economy.

"While of course we can't pick up the debts of a registered charity, we do want to ensure the festival goes ahead next year.

"We will therefore be working with local promoters, venues, and other stakeholders, and drawing upon the expertise of our own festivals and De Montfort Hall teams, to ensure that an interim comedy festival programme can take place in 2027, while we work to secure a sustainable operation for the long-term."

The most recent edition of the festival was held in February and featured more than 500 acts across multiple venues.

However, it then emerged hundreds of performers had not been paid for their work.

They included comedian Benjamin Alborough, who told the BBC he was owed almost £2,000.

Organisers said in May the delay was due to cashflow problems but they were aiming to honour the payments as quickly as possible.

Michael Day, an official from performing arts union Equity, said: "Despite being widely anticipated, it's a huge blow to see Leicester Comedy Festival file for insolvency.

"It's terrible news and leaves many performers unpaid from this year's festival.

"At Equity, we've been supporting many comedians who were left unpaid and we have secured payment for several of them.

"However, getting money owed to comedians will become far more difficult under an insolvency."

The Live Comedy Association - set up to support people working in grassroots live comedy - says it has launched a crowdfunding campaign to raise money to support those affected by non-payments.

It added the initial target was £30,000, with all funds raised going directly towards assisting individuals, promoters, venues and staff who were owed money.

The association's director Jessica Toomey said: "We are incredibly sad about the dreadful impact this will have on many of our members and the wider live comedy sector across the UK."

articles.title: Tributes paid to 'quietly seismic' theatre director and playwright Peter Gill
articles.text:
Theatre director, playwright and actor Peter Gill, who has died aged 86, has been described as a "gentle man with a fierce intelligence" who had a "quietly seismic" influence on British theatre.

Cardiff-born Gill performed with the Royal Shakespeare Company and appeared in films including HMS Defiant and Zulu before embarking on a successful theatre directing career.

Among those to pay tribute was Welsh actor Luke Evans, who credited Gill with launching his own career.

Gill's agent Mel Kenyon said his work had a "rare emotional delicacy" that was "beautifully observed and finely tuned".

Gill is closely associated with his work at the Royal Court in London, where he is credited with introducing the plays of English writer DH Lawrence to the theatrical world.

Born in Cardiff on 7 September 1939, he was raised in a working-class community and remained "fiercely proud of his Welsh heritage throughout his life", according to an obituary written by his agency Casarotto Ramsay & Associates.

He pursued an acting career from the age of 18 before moving into theatre, most closely associated with the Royal Court, where he championed three Lawrence plays A Collier's Friday Night, The Daughter-in-Law and The Widowing of Mrs Holroyd.

"Their success revived interest in Lawrence's dramatic work and helped spark a renaissance of his plays in London theatre circles after decades of relative obscurity following his death in 1930," the agency said.

He also presented two of his early plays, The Sleeper's Den and Over Gardens Out, at the theatre, before becoming associate director in 1970.

In 1976, he became artistic director of Riverside Studios, with his production of William Shakespeare's As You Like It marking the official opening of the Hammersmith-based theatre that year.

He also adapted Anton Chekhov's The Cherry Orchard for the theatre, helping transform it from a "small fringe theatre" into a "venue regarded as the equal of the leading theatres of the West End".

In 1980, he was appointed OBE for his services to theatre, also founding the National Theatre Studio in 1984 and running it until 1990.

Kenyon described Gill as a "gentle man with a fierce intelligence" and a "voracious reader" with an "expansive knowledge of the arts".

"Whenever we talked, I walked away a wiser person. He taught me so much just by being him. He was a singular man, a kind, generous and curious man. I will miss him greatly," Kenyon said.

Theatre director and producer Michael Grandage said he believed Gill's contribution to British theatre "will come to be regarded as quietly seismic".

"Through the observation of the domestic, he always gave us something universal," he said, adding that future generations discovering his work would come across "some of the finest plays written in the last 70 years with unquestionably some of the most beautiful prose in the English language".

Welsh actor Luke Evans also paid tribute to Gill in a post to Instagram, remembering the theatre director for changing the trajectory of his career after casting him in a 2008 revival of Small Change.

Over a black and white photo of the thespian, Evans - known for his roles in The Hobbit and Beauty and the Beast - wrote: "This man gave me a role in a play when I was 27 that changed my whole professional life.

"Peter Gill has passed away at 86 leaving behind a legacy of work that I was very lucky enough to be a small part of.

"Without that play Small Change that he wrote and directed me in, I don't think I would have ever had a film career, or any career to be honest.

"RIP dear Peter and thank you."

Tamara Harvey, co-artistic director of the Royal Shakespeare Company, said Gill was a "true artist and tirelessly devoted to the theatre".

"His unerring ability to capture the complexity of human existence will live on in his writing but he will, nevertheless, be deeply missed," she said.
